claim: Premotor projection neurons in the cortical song nucleus HVC (HVCRA neurons) are necessary for producing learned song in songbirds.
source: In songbirds, premotor projection neurons in the cortical song nucleus HVC are necessary for producing learned song and exhibit precise sequential activity during singing.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work establishing necessity of HVCRA neurons for song production

claim: HVCRA neurons exhibit precise sequential activity during singing.
source: In songbirds, premotor projection neurons in the cortical song nucleus HVC are necessary for producing learned song and exhibit precise sequential activity during singing.
evidence: Supported by citations and data presented in the manuscript

claim: Populations of HVC premotor neurons are associated with the beginning and ending of singing-related neural sequences.
source: Using cell-type specific calcium imaging we identify populations of HVC premotor neurons associated with the beginning and ending of singing-related neural sequences.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in the manuscript

claim: Neuronal populations transition from sparse preparatory activity prior to song to precise neural sequences during singing.
source: We characterize neurons that bookend singing-related sequences and neuronal populations that transition from sparse preparatory activity prior to song to precise neural sequences during singing.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing activity patterns before and during song

claim: Pre-song activity may be involved in motor preparation to sing.
source: Recordings from downstream premotor neurons or the respiratory system suggest that pre-song activity may be involved in motor preparation to sing.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings and respiratory measurements

claim: Precise neural sequences begin and end as part of orchestrated activity across functionally diverse populations of cortical premotor neurons.
source: These findings reveal population mechanisms associated with moving from non-vocal to vocal behavioral states and suggest that precise neural sequences begin and end as part of orchestrated activity across functionally diverse populations of cortical premotor neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the population-level calcium imaging data showing coordinated activity patterns

claim: Neural sequences develop through experience.
source: Neural sequences develop through experience and have been described in several brain areas, including the motor cortex, hippocampus, cerebellum, and the basal ganglia (Barnes et al., 2005; Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Harvey et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2009; Li et al., 2015; Luczak et al., 2007; Mauk and Buonomano, 2004; Peters et al., 2014; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2015; Schwartz and Moran, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Our understanding of sequence initiation and termination is still limited.
source: Although computational models provide important insights into circuit architectures capable of sustaining sequenced activity (Churchland et al., 2010b; Fiete et al., 2004; Fiete et al., 2010; Haga and Fukai, 2018; Harvey et al., 2012; Kumar et al., 2010; Rajan et al., 2016), our understanding of sequence initiation and termination is still limited.
evidence: Reflects established scientific knowledge and gaps in the field

claim: HVCRA neurons are thought to only be active during vocal production in waking adult birds.
source: HVCRA neurons are thought to only be active during vocal production in waking adult birds, yet ~50% of recorded HVCRA neurons do not exhibit any activity during singing (Hahnloser et al., 2002; Hamaguchi et al., 2016; Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007; Long et al., 2010; Lynch et al., 2016), leaving the function of much of the HVCRA circuitry unresolved.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies

claim: Approximately 50% of recorded HVCRA neurons do not exhibit any activity during singing.
source: HVCRA neurons are thought to only be active during vocal production in waking adult birds, yet ~50% of recorded HVCRA neurons do not exhibit any activity during singing (Hahnloser et al., 2002; Hamaguchi et al., 2016; Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007; Long et al., 2010; Lynch et al., 2016), leaving the function of much of the HVCRA circuitry unresolved.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies

claim: The function of much of the HVCRA circuitry is unresolved.
source: HVCRA neurons are thought to only be active during vocal production in waking adult birds, yet ~50% of recorded HVCRA neurons do not exhibit any activity during singing (Hahnloser et al., 2002; Hamaguchi et al., 2016; Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007; Long et al., 2010; Lynch et al., 2016), leaving the function of much of the HVCRA circuitry unresolved.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that many HVCRA neurons are inactive during singing

claim: Multi-unit recordings from HVC show increases in activity tens to hundreds of milliseconds prior to singing.
source: Multi-unit recordings from HVC, which are typically dominated by the activity of interneurons, show increases in activity tens to hundreds of milliseconds prior to singing (Crandall et al., 2007; Day et al., 2009; Rajan, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies

claim: HVCAv neurons become active immediately prior to song onset.
source: Calcium imaging from HVCAv neurons and electrophysiological recordings from HVCX neurons indicate that they also become active immediately prior to song onset (Rajan, 2018; Roberts et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous calcium imaging and electrophysiological studies

claim: HVCX neurons become active immediately prior to song onset.
source: Calcium imaging from HVCAv neurons and electrophysiological recordings from HVCX neurons indicate that they also become active immediately prior to song onset (Rajan, 2018; Roberts et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous calcium imaging and electrophysiological studies

claim: A total of 223 HVCRA neurons were imaged during production of 1298 song syllables from six birds.
source: A total of 223 HVCRA neurons were imaged during production of 1298 song syllables from six birds (30 song phrases across 18 imaging trials, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental data collected

claim: The approach used exclusively and uniformly labeled populations of HVCRA neurons.
source: Although this did not label all RA projecting neurons in HVC, we found that this approach exclusively and uniformly labeled populations of HVCRA neurons (Figure 1c–f).
evidence: Supported by histological verification shown in Figure 1

claim: Birds engaged in singing on average 24 s (±49 s) after a female bird was presented.
source: On average, birds engaged in singing in 24 s (±49 s) of a female bird being presented.
evidence: Direct measurement from behavioral observations

claim: The average rise time of calcium events was 0.112 ± 0.047 s SD.
source: Given the slow decay times of calcium signals relative to singing behavior, we defined neuronal activity by the rise times of calcium events that were >3 standard deviations (SD) above baseline (Figure 1g, average rise time: 0.112 ± 0.047 s SD, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Direct measurement from calcium imaging data

claim: The activity of individual HVCRA neurons was time-locked to a moment in the birds' song.
source: The activity of individual HVCRA neurons was time-locked to a moment in the birds' song, with different neurons active at different moments in the song motif (Figure 1g–h; onset jitter = 55.0 ± 60.9 ms, populations imaged at 30 frames per second).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing temporal precision

claim: The onset jitter of HVCRA neuron activity was 55.0 ± 60.9 ms.
source: The activity of individual HVCRA neurons was time-locked to a moment in the birds' song, with different neurons active at different moments in the song motif (Figure 1g–h; onset jitter = 55.0 ± 60.9 ms, populations imaged at 30 frames per second).
evidence: Direct measurement from calcium imaging data

claim: The sequential activity of HVCRA neurons roughly coded for all moments in the song motif.
source: We found that the sequential activity of HVCRA neurons roughly coded for all moments in the song motif (Figure 1h).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing distributed activity across the motif

claim: 30 out of 30 song phrases from six birds exhibited 'peri-song' activity.
source: 30 out of 30 song phrases from six birds exhibited 'peri-song' activity, defined as the 5 s intervals before and after singing, plus silent gaps within song phrases.
evidence: Direct count from experimental observations

claim: 54.3% of neurons were active during peri-song intervals.
source: Slightly fewer HVCRA neurons were active during peri-song intervals (54.3% of neurons) than during singing (59.9%), (t = −1.1, p=0.29 two-sample t test; Figure 2b).
evidence: Direct measurement from calcium imaging data with statistical test

claim: 59.9% of neurons were active during singing.
source: Slightly fewer HVCRA neurons were active during peri-song intervals (54.3% of neurons) than during singing (59.9%), (t = −1.1, p=0.29 two-sample t test; Figure 2b).
evidence: Direct measurement from calcium imaging data with statistical test

claim: There was no significant difference in the percentage of neurons active during peri-song intervals versus singing (p=0.29).
source: Slightly fewer HVCRA neurons were active during peri-song intervals (54.3% of neurons) than during singing (59.9%), (t = −1.1, p=0.29 two-sample t test; Figure 2b).
evidence: Statistical test result from calcium imaging data

claim: Of the neurons active during peri-song intervals, 40.6% were active prior to song onset.
source: Of the neurons that were active during peri-song intervals, 40.6% were active prior to song onset, 17.8% were active following song offset, and 41.6% were active before and after song (N = 197 neurons, six birds, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct measurement from calcium imaging data

claim: Of the neurons active during peri-song intervals, 17.8% were active following song offset.
source: Of the neurons that were active during peri-song intervals, 40.6% were active prior to song onset, 17.8% were active following song offset, and 41.6% were active before and after song (N = 197 neurons, six birds, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct measurement from calcium imaging data

claim: Of the neurons active during peri-song intervals, 41.6% were active before and after song.
source: Of the neurons that were active during peri-song intervals, 40.6% were active prior to song onset, 17.8% were active following song offset, and 41.6% were active before and after song (N = 197 neurons, six birds, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct measurement from calcium imaging data

claim: Neuronal populations displayed considerably more calcium events during song than during peri-song periods.
source: Although neuronal populations displayed considerably more calcium events during song (t = 5.635, p=5.65×10−7 two-sample t, normalized song event rate = 24.09 events/s±15.95 SD, normalized peri-song event rate = 6.97 events/s±3.72 SD), a substantial fraction of all recorded calcium events occurred within the 5 s intervals before or after song (997/2366 or 32.5% of all calcium events).
evidence: Statistical comparison of event rates with p-value

claim: The normalized song event rate was 24.09 events/s±15.95 SD.
source: Although neuronal populations displayed considerably more calcium events during song (t = 5.635, p=5.65×10−7 two-sample t, normalized song event rate = 24.09 events/s±15.95 SD, normalized peri-song event rate = 6.97 events/s±3.72 SD), a substantial fraction of all recorded calcium events occurred within the 5 s intervals before or after song (997/2366 or 32.5% of all calcium events).
evidence: Direct measurement from calcium imaging data

claim: The normalized peri-song event rate was 6.97 events/s±3.72 SD.
source: Although neuronal populations displayed considerably more calcium events during song (t = 5.635, p=5.65×10−7 two-sample t, normalized song event rate = 24.09 events/s±15.95 SD, normalized peri-song event rate = 6.97 events/s±3.72 SD), a substantial fraction of all recorded calcium events occurred within the 5 s intervals before or after song (997/2366 or 32.5% of all calcium events).
evidence: Direct measurement from calcium imaging data

claim: 32.5% of all calcium events occurred within the 5 s intervals before or after song.
source: Although neuronal populations displayed considerably more calcium events during song (t = 5.635, p=5.65×10−7 two-sample t, normalized song event rate = 24.09 events/s±15.95 SD, normalized peri-song event rate = 6.97 events/s±3.72 SD), a substantial fraction of all recorded calcium events occurred within the 5 s intervals before or after song (997/2366 or 32.5% of all calcium events).
evidence: Direct calculation from calcium imaging data

claim: HVCRA phrase indices were not uniformly distributed.
source: We found that HVCRA phrase indices were not uniformly distributed (χ2 (7, N = 223)=46.3, p=7.6×10−8, Chi-square goodness of fit test), with a significant fraction (36%) falling at the extremes of this scale (Figure 2d), and that neurons with different phrase indices were anatomically intermingled throughout HVC (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Statistical test result from phrase index analysis

claim: 36% of neurons had phrase indices falling at the extremes of the scale.
source: We found that HVCRA phrase indices were not uniformly distributed (χ2 (7, N = 223)=46.3, p=7.6×10−8, Chi-square goodness of fit test), with a significant fraction (36%) falling at the extremes of this scale (Figure 2d), and that neurons with different phrase indices were anatomically intermingled throughout HVC (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct calculation from phrase index data

claim: Neurons with different phrase indices were anatomically intermingled throughout HVC.
source: We found that HVCRA phrase indices were not uniformly distributed (χ2 (7, N = 223)=46.3, p=7.6×10−8, Chi-square goodness of fit test), with a significant fraction (36%) falling at the extremes of this scale (Figure 2d), and that neurons with different phrase indices were anatomically intermingled throughout HVC (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by anatomical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: 64.1% of neurons displayed sparse heterogenous activity during peri-song periods and transitioned to temporally precise activity during singing (pan-song neurons).
source: Most neurons (64.1%) displayed sparse heterogenous activity during peri-song periods and transitioned to temporally precise activity during singing (referred to here as 'pan-song neurons'; Figure 2—figure supplement 5; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Direct calculation from calcium imaging data

claim: 18.4% of neurons were exclusively active during peri-song intervals (peri-song neurons).
source: At the extremes of the phrase index scale (phrase indices −1 or +1), we found that 18.4% of neurons were exclusively active during peri-song intervals (phrase index = −1, referred to here as 'peri-song neurons'; Supplementary file 2), while 17.5% participated exclusively in neural sequences during singing (phrase index =+1, referred to here as 'song neurons'; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Direct calculation from phrase index data

claim: 17.5% of neurons participated exclusively in neural sequences during singing (song neurons).
source: At the extremes of the phrase index scale (phrase indices −1 or +1), we found that 18.4% of neurons were exclusively active during peri-song intervals (phrase index = −1, referred to here as 'peri-song neurons'; Supplementary file 2), while 17.5% participated exclusively in neural sequences during singing (phrase index =+1, referred to here as 'song neurons'; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Direct calculation from phrase index data

claim: HVCRA neurons were significantly more active during the peri-song periods than baseline.
source: This was not the case, however, as HVCRA neurons were largely inactive outside of peri-song intervals and were significantly more active during the peri-song periods than baseline (baseline calculated from periods ≥ 10 s removed from periods of singing or calling, p=8.4×10−5, Chi-square = 18.78 Friedman test, baseline = 12.9% ± 5.7 SD of fluorescence values normalized to song, pre-song = 26.9% ± 14.7, and post-song = 30.2% ± 10.7).
evidence: Statistical test result comparing peri-song activity to baseline

claim: Peri-song calcium events were larger in amplitude than events occurring during song.
source: In addition, we examined the amplitudes of peri-song calcium events and found that they were larger than events occurring during song (t = 3.2769, p=0.0012, two-tailed t test, 279 fluorescence peaks measured from neurons active during both peri-song and song, pan-song neurons with phrase indices between −0.18 to 0.18).
evidence: Statistical comparison of calcium event amplitudes

claim: Pre-song activity was found in 28/30 song phrases analyzed.
source: We found pre-song activity in 28/30 song phrases analyzed.
evidence: Direct count from experimental observations

claim: 96.2% of calcium events occurred more than 100 ms prior to vocal onset.
source: The vast majority of pre-song activity we describe occurs hundreds of milliseconds to seconds prior to vocalizations, suggesting a role in planning or preparation to vocalize (96.2% of calcium events occurred more than 100 ms prior to vocal onset and 65.6% occurred more than 1 s prior to vocal onset).
evidence: Direct calculation from timing of calcium events

claim: 65.6% of calcium events occurred more than 1 s prior to vocal onset.
source: The vast majority of pre-song activity we describe occurs hundreds of milliseconds to seconds prior to vocalizations, suggesting a role in planning or preparation to vocalize (96.2% of calcium events occurred more than 100 ms prior to vocal onset and 65.6% occurred more than 1 s prior to vocal onset).
evidence: Direct calculation from timing of calcium events

claim: There was no correlation between pre-song event rates and the number of introductory notes.
source: Pre-song activity (prior to introductory notes) could be related to the number of introductory notes to be sung, but we found no correlation between pre-song event rates and the number of introductory notes (Figure 2—figure supplement 10).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing lack of correlation

claim: In 27/28 song phrases, increases in population activity greater than 3 SDs above baseline predicted song onset within the following 4–5 s.
source: In 27/28 song phrases we found increases in population activity greater than 3 SDs above baseline predicted song onset within the following 4–5 s (2.44 s ± 1.0 s SD, 28 song phrases from five birds).
evidence: Direct measurement from calcium imaging data

claim: The average time between increased population activity and song onset was 2.44 s ± 1.0 s SD.
source: In 27/28 song phrases we found increases in population activity greater than 3 SDs above baseline predicted song onset within the following 4–5 s (2.44 s ± 1.0 s SD, 28 song phrases from five birds).
evidence: Direct measurement from calcium imaging data

claim: HVCRA neuron activity is predictive of the voluntary production of courtship song.
source: Together, these results indicate that HVCRA neuron activity is predictive of the voluntary production of courtship song and suggests a role for this network in motor planning and in preparation to sing.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal relationship between pre-song activity and song onset

claim: 41 out of 223 neurons were active exclusively before or after singing (peri-song neurons).
source: A substantial fraction of all imaged neurons (41/223 neurons) were active exclusively before or after singing (Figure 2d, neurons with a phrase index of −1).
evidence: Direct count from calcium imaging data

claim: The number of active peri-song neurons and the density of calcium events increased 1–3 s prior to song onset.
source: Both the number of active peri-song neurons and the density of calcium events increased 1–3 s prior to song onset, with the event rate peaking 1.5 s prior to singing (Figure 3b–c,i) and then declining sharply in the last second before song onset (Figure 3i).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3

claim: The event rate of peri-song neurons peaked 1.5 s prior to singing.
source: Both the number of active peri-song neurons and the density of calcium events increased 1–3 s prior to song onset, with the event rate peaking 1.5 s prior to singing (Figure 3b–c,i) and then declining sharply in the last second before song onset (Figure 3i).
evidence: Direct measurement from calcium imaging data

claim: 143 out of 223 neurons were pan-song neurons.
source: Most of the neurons we imaged, pan-song neurons (143/223 neurons), exhibited sparse, heterogeneous activity before and/or after song and exhibited time-locked sequences during singing (Figure 3d–f).
evidence: Direct count from calcium imaging data

claim: Pan-song neurons exhibited substantial increases in their activity in the last ~2 s prior to song onset.
source: Pan-song neurons exhibited substantial increases in their activity in the last ~2 s prior to song onset.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data

claim: The activity of pan-song neurons continued to increase as the activity of peri-song neurons began to ramp-off prior to song onset.
source: Their activity continued to increase as the activity of peri-song neurons began to ramp-off prior to song onset (Figure 3g,I, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing temporal dynamics

claim: There were differences in pre-song activity profiles between peri-song and pan-song neurons.
source: Differences in pre-song activity profiles between peri-song and pan-song neurons (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, K-S test, k = 0.26, p=0.056) may support temporally coordinated network transitions as birds prepare to sing, suggesting that neural sequences for song could emerge as part of changing network dynamics in HVC.
evidence: Statistical test result comparing activity profiles

claim: Pan-song and song neurons had a similar probability of being active within each motif.
source: We found that pan-song and song neurons had a similar probability of being active within each motif (song neurons probability of at least one calcium event per motif P(motif)=0.72 ± 0.32, pan-song neurons P(motif)=0.66 ± 0.29, K-S test, p=0.11; Figure 3—figure supplement 3); however, we also noted that the probability of being active was lower than in electrophysiological recordings (Hahnloser et al., 2002; Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007).
evidence: Statistical comparison of activity probabilities

claim: There was no difference in signal to noise ratio between pan-song neurons and song neurons during singing.
source: To better understand this, we calculated signal to noise ratios (SNRs, signal defined as peak fluorescence of calcium events during song) between pan-song neurons and song neurons during singing (SNR song neurons = 913.8 ± 405.4 (7 neurons), pan-song neurons = 638.3 ± 248.2 SEM, n = 36 neurons). We found no difference in SNR between these neurons (two-sample t test, p=0.6; SNR calculated from 156 calcium events (28 from song neurons and 128 from pan-song neurons), suggesting that although we are underestimating activity during singing, these limitations are unlikely to obscure differences between pan-song and song neurons.
evidence: Statistical comparison of SNR values

claim: Within 5 s after song offset, peri-song neurons exhibited a sharp increase in activity followed by a gradual ramp-off.
source: Within 5 s after song offset, peri-song neurons exhibited a sharp increase in activity followed by a gradual ramp-off (Figure 3a–c,h,j, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2) whereas pan-song neurons only exhibited a ramp-off (Figure 3d–f,h,j).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3

claim: The distribution of post-song activity differed between peri-song and pan-song neurons.
source: Although the distribution of post-song activity differed between peri-song and pan-song neurons (K-S test, k = 0.2692, p=0.0373), both populations returned to baseline activity over similar timescales.
evidence: Statistical test result comparing post-song activity distributions

claim: There was no significant correlation between the duration of song phrases and the number of active neurons in the post-song period.
source: To explore this idea, we examined whether the duration of song phrases was correlated with the number of active neurons in the post-song period, but did not find a significant correlation (r2 = 0.03).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing lack of correlation

claim: Pre-song activity forecasts impending song.
source: Although the function of post-song activity is unclear, our results indicate that pre-song activity forecasts impending song and suggest a previously unappreciated role for the HVCRA network in planning or preparing to sing.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal relationship between pre-song activity and song onset

claim: Robust preparatory activity was identified several hundreds of milliseconds prior to song onset in HVC of Bengalese finches.
source: Using multi-channel neural recordings in HVC, we identified robust preparatory activity several hundreds of milliseconds prior to song onset (Figure 4a–g).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4

claim: The pre-song and song-related multiunit spike rates in Bengalese finches were significantly above baseline.
source: The pre-song and song–related multiunit spike rates were significantly above baseline (Wilcoxon signed-rank test after Bonferroni correction, n = 29 MU sites. pre-song: z = 4.62, p=0.030; song: z = 4.70, p<0.001), whereas the post-song spike rates was not (z = 2.17, p=0.089).
evidence: Statistical test results from electrophysiological recordings

claim: Pre-song activity in Bengalese finches increased above baseline −1.47 ± 1.05 s prior to song onset.
source: Pre-song activity increased above baseline −1.47 ± 1.05 s prior to song onset, a timescale that closely matched the timing of peak calcium-event rates in peri-song neurons in zebra finches.
evidence: Direct measurement from electrophysiological recordings

claim: The offset timing of post-song activity in Bengalese finches was 0.42 ± 0.23 s.
source: The offset timing of post-song activity was 0.42 ± 0.23 s.
evidence: Direct measurement from electrophysiological recordings

claim: Preparatory activity in HVC is a common network motif important for song generation and the onset of precise neural sequences.
source: This indicates that preparatory activity in HVC is a common network motif important for song generation and the onset of precise neural sequences.
evidence: Inferred from observations in both zebra finches and Bengalese finches

claim: The CVISI for RA neurons changed significantly during song, reaching higher values during pre-song, song, and post-song epochs as compared to spontaneous activity.
source: As expected, we did not find substantial differences in spike rates between non-singing and singing states (not shown) but found that the CVISI for RA neurons changed significantly during song, reaching higher values during pre-song, song, and post-song epochs as compared to spontaneous activity (Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, p<0.005, two-sided K-S tests).
evidence: Statistical test results from electrophysiological recordings in RA

claim: HVCRA sequences associated with preparation to sing propagate to downstream premotor circuits prior to song onset.
source: This suggests that HVCRA sequences associated with preparation to sing propagate to downstream premotor circuits prior to song onset and that HVC continues to influence descending motor pathways following song cessation.
evidence: Inferred from changes in RA neuron activity during pre-song and post-song periods

claim: During singing, birds significantly accelerated the respiratory rhythm.
source: During singing, birds significantly accelerated the respiratory rhythm and marginally shifted towards longer periods of expiration during each cycle (Figure 6b, respiratory duration pre-song = 0.38 ± 0.04 s (SD), song = 0.18 ± 0.03 s, post-song = 0.39 ± 0.06 s: F(2,10) = 46.63, p<0.001; duty cycle (% of time in expiration) pre-song = 58% ± 3 (SEM), song = 57% ± 2.5, post-song = 61% ± 2.4: F(2,10) = 3.56, p=0.07).
evidence: Statistical test results from respiratory measurements

claim: Respiratory cycle duration significantly accelerated in the last second prior to song onset.
source: We found that significant changes in respiration also preceded song onset. Respiratory cycle duration significantly accelerated in the last second prior to song onset with relative decreases of expiratory phases (respiratory duration: F(3,15) = 7.67, p=0.02, duty cycle: F(3,15) = 4.077, p=0.07; Figure 6d).
evidence: Statistical test results from respiratory measurements

claim: Following song termination, birds immediately returned to longer respiratory cycles.
source: Following song termination, birds immediately returned to longer respiratory cycles but during the first second post-song, they spent more time exhaling compared to inhaling, a behavior likely involved in helping to recover from singing-related hyperventilation (respiratory duration: F(2,10) = 0.509, p<n .s., duty cycle: F(2,10) = 6.553, p<0. 01; Figure 6e).
evidence: Statistical test results from respiratory measurements

claim: Changes in respiration during the last second before and first second following song support the idea that HVCRA neurons provide descending motor commands that coordinate transitions between non-vocal and vocal states by coordinating respiratory patterns.
source: These changes in respiration during the last second before and first second following song support the idea that HVCRA neurons provide descending motor commands that coordinate transitions between non-vocal and vocal states by coordinating respiratory patterns.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal relationship between HVCRA activity and respiratory changes

claim: Pre-song activity 1–3 s prior to song onset may reflect motor planning or the decision to sing, rather than respiratory preparation.
source: The lack of changes at earlier time-points prior to singing also indicate that pre-song activity 1–3 s prior to song onset may reflect motor planning or the decision to sing, rather than respiratory preparation.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of respiratory changes at earlier time points

claim: HVCRA neurons could function in aspects of motor planning as well as preparation.
source: Together these, findings support the idea that HVCRA neurons could function in aspects of motor planning as well as preparation.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal dynamics of pre-song activity and respiratory changes

claim: Previous studies suggested that the HVCRA network functions as a time-keeper, encoding motif-level temporal representations of song via propagation of precisely timed neural sequences.
source: Previous studies suggested that the HVCRA network functions as a time-keeper, encoding motif-level temporal representations of song via propagation of precisely timed neural sequences (Hahnloser et al., 2002; Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007; Long and Fee, 2008; Long et al., 2010; Lynch et al., 2016; Markowitz et al., 2015; Picardo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Neural sequences among HVCRA neurons emerge as part of orchestrated population activity across a larger network of HVCRA neurons.
source: Our principal result is that neural sequences among HVCRA neurons emerge as part of orchestrated population activity across a larger network of HVCRA neurons.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing coordinated activity patterns

claim: Peri-song and pan-song HVCRA neurons forecast the start of singing.
source: Peri-song and pan-song HVCRA neurons forecast the start of singing.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing pre-song activity

claim: Preparatory activity in HVCRA neurons precedes the pre-bout activity described in other classes of HVC neurons and other portions of the song system.
source: Moreover, we find that preparatory activity in HVCRA neurons precedes the pre-bout activity described in other classes of HVC neurons and other portions of the song system previously described in zebra finches (Danish et al., 2017; Goldberg et al., 2010; Goldberg and Fee, 2012; Kao et al., 2008; Rajan, 2018; Roberts et al., 2017; Vyssotski et al., 2016; Williams and Vicario, 1993) and described here in Bengalese finches (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by comparison of timing with previous studies and current data

claim: HVCRA neurons may seed network wide changes among other classes of HVC neurons and the song system more generally.
source: This suggests that HVCRA neurons may seed network wide changes among other classes of HVC neurons and the song system more generally.
evidence: Inferred from the early timing of HVCRA preparatory activity

claim: Preparatory activity in populations of HVCRA neurons drives descending motor commands via RA and its connections to the ventral respiratory group and syringeal motoneurons in the medulla.
source: Preparatory activity in populations of HVCRA neurons drives descending motor commands via RA and its connections to the ventral respiratory group and syringeal motoneurons in the medulla (Andalman et al., 2011; Goller and Cooper, 2004; Roberts et al., 2008; Sturdy et al., 2003; Suthers et al., 1999; Wild, 1993).
evidence: Supported by data and citations to anatomical studies

claim: Only population activity is sufficient to drive bursting in RA, given the sparsity of HVCRA neuron activity and the convergence of HVCRA input to RA.
source: Given the sparsity of HVCRA neuron activity and the convergence of HVCRA input to RA, it is likely that only population activity, like that described here, is sufficient to drive bursting in RA.
evidence: Inferred from known circuit properties and observed activity patterns

claim: Recurrent projections from the brainstem update activity in HVC and trigger the initiation of neural sequences once the periphery is readied for the first respiratory cycle for song.
source: Because the initiation of singing requires precise coordination between respiratory state and descending motor commands, we hypothesize that recurrent projections from the brainstem update activity in HVC and trigger the initiation of neural sequences once the periphery is readied for the first respiratory cycle for song (Ashmore et al., 2005; Hamaguchi et al., 2016; Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: Hypothesized based on known anatomy and functional requirements, supported by citations

claim: Circuitry related to recurrent projections into HVC increase their activity tens of milliseconds prior to song onset.
source: Circuitry related to recurrent projections into HVC increase their activity tens of milliseconds prior to song onset (Danish et al., 2017; Vyssotski et al., 2016; Williams and Vicario, 1993) and thus may provide final inputs that help mediate the transition from heterogenous preparatory activity to the precisely sequenced activity that underlies song.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: HVC receives input from cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain.
source: HVC receives input from cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain (Li and Sakaguchi, 1997; Shea et al., 2010; Shea and Margoliash, 2003), noradrenergic neurons in the locus coeruleus (Appeltants et al., 2000), and dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain (Hamaguchi and Mooney, 2012; Tanaka et al., 2018), any or all of which could play potent roles in shifting the excitability of subsets of HVCRA involved in song preparation and initiation.
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies

claim: HVC receives input from noradrenergic neurons in the locus coeruleus.

evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies

evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies

evidence: Speculative inference based on known neuromodulatory inputs

claim: It is not yet known whether activity occurring among peri-song and pan-song HVCRA neurons prior to song onset is necessary for song initiation or production.
source: Although it is not yet known whether activity occuring among peri-song and pan-song HVCRA neurons prior to song onset is necessary for song initiation or production, previous studies have identified pyramidal tract neurons (PTupper) in the anterior lateral motor cortex that play a specific role in motor planning (Economo et al., 2018).
evidence: Acknowledges limitation of current study

claim: PTupper neurons in the anterior lateral motor cortex are active prior to movement onset and show decreased activity during movement.
source: These neurons are active prior to movement onset and show decreased activity during movement, similar to the activity of HVCRA peri-song neurons described here.
evidence: Comparison to previous findings in mammalian motor cortex

claim: PTupper neurons are hypothesized to encode cognitive signals related to motor planning.
source: PTupper neurons innervate the thalamus rather than medulla and are hypothesized to encode cognitive signals related to motor planning (Economo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: RA provides inputs to the medulla and the thalamus.
source: Likewise, RA provides inputs to the medulla and the thalamus (Goldberg and Fee, 2012; Roberts et al., 2008; Vates et al., 1997; Wild, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies

claim: It is currently not known if subpopulations of RA neurons project exclusively to the thalamus.
source: However, it is currently not known if subpopulations of RA neurons project exclusively to the thalamus or if peri-song and pan-song HVCRA neurons have unique downstream targets within RA.
evidence: Acknowledges gap in current knowledge

claim: It is currently not known if peri-song and pan-song HVCRA neurons have unique downstream targets within RA.
source: However, it is currently not known if subpopulations of RA neurons project exclusively to the thalamus or if peri-song and pan-song HVCRA neurons have unique downstream targets within RA.
evidence: Acknowledges gap in current knowledge

claim: Neural activity associated with motor planning and preparation has been observed in motor and premotor cortices for a variety of different motor tasks in rodents and primates.
source: Neural activity associated with motor planning and preparation has been observed in motor and premotor cortices for a variety of different motor tasks in rodents and primates (Chen et al., 2017; Churchland et al., 2010a; Churchland et al., 2006a; Churchland et al., 2006b; Economo et al., 2018; Inagaki et al., 2019; Kaufman et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016; Murakami and Mainen, 2015; Murakami et al., 2014; Tanji and Evarts, 1976), including vocalizations (Gavrilov et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by extensive citations to previous literature

claim: Pre-movement activity is thought to reflect the decision to perform movements and is characterized by a high degree of variability from trial to trial.
source: This activity is thought to reflect the decision to perform movements and is characterized by a high degree of variability from trial to trial.
evidence: Reflects established understanding in the field

claim: Changes in circuit dynamics function to shift the initial state of a network to levels that enable efficient and accurate motor performances.
source: Changes in circuit dynamics function to shift the initial state of a network to levels that enable efficient and accurate motor performances and this activity can start to unfold seconds prior to movement initiation (Churchland et al., 2010a; Inagaki et al., 2019; Murakami and Mainen, 2015; Svoboda and Li, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: HVC is proposed to be analogous to the mammalian motor cortex (layer III neurons of the primary motor cortex).
source: HVC is proposed to be analogous to the mammalian motor cortex (layer III neurons of the primary motor cortex) (Pfenning et al., 2014), or premotor cortex (Bolhuis et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous comparative studies

claim: Pre-movement activity is a common mechanism for ensuring the accurate production of volitional behaviors.
source: Our observation of preparatory activity seconds before the onset of courtship song in two different songbird species suggests that pre-movement activity is a common mechanism for ensuring the accurate production of volitional behaviors.
evidence: Inferred from observations in both zebra finches and Bengalese finches

claim: Individual HVCRA neurons exhibit a high degree of trial to trial variability.
source: In line with recordings of pre-motor activity in mammals, individual HVCRA neurons exhibit a high degree of trial to trial variability.
evidence: Observed in calcium imaging data

claim: Recording of preparatory activity across larger populations of HVCRA neurons may be useful for decoding trial to trial variability in song structure.
source: Recording of preparatory activity across larger populations of HVCRA neurons may be useful for decoding this trial to trial variability in song structure, ultimately providing a predictive readout of impending behaviors.
evidence: Speculative suggestion for future research

claim: Sequential activation of neurons is thought to provide computational advantages for encoding temporal information associated with episodic memories or behavioral sequences.
source: Sequential activation of neurons is thought to provide computational advantages for encoding temporal information associated with episodic memories or behavioral sequences (Fiete et al., 2004; Kumar et al., 2010; Rajan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical and computational studies

claim: Neural sequences in HVC provide one of the cleanest examples linking brain activity with a naturally learned and volitionally produced skilled motor behavior.
source: Neural sequences in HVC provide one of the cleanest examples linking brain activity with a naturally learned and volitionally produced skilled motor behavior (Fee et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation and established knowledge in the field

claim: The study provides a glimpse of how neural sequences emerge through temporally coordinated transitions within a potentially hierarchically organized network.
source: Our study provides a glimpse of how these sequences emerge through temporally coordinated transitions within a potentially hierarchically organized network and suggests a general framework for initiating the production of skilled motor behaviors.
evidence: Summary inference from the study's findings
